consumer_seed: The Ofcom automatic-compensation guide was published on 12 March 2024.
The Ofcom automatic-compensation guide was last updated on 20 July 2026.
The scheme provides money back from participating broadband and landline providers when specified problems occur, without the customer having to ask.
BT was listed by Ofcom as signed up to the automatic compensation scheme.
EE was listed by Ofcom as signed up to the automatic compensation scheme.
Hyperoptic was listed by Ofcom as signed up to the automatic compensation scheme.
Plusnet was listed by Ofcom as signed up to the automatic compensation scheme.
Sky, including NOW Broadband was listed by Ofcom as signed up to the automatic compensation scheme.
TalkTalk, subject to restrictions for customers not on the Openreach network was listed by Ofcom as signed up to the automatic compensation scheme.
Utility Warehouse was listed by Ofcom as signed up to the automatic compensation scheme.
Virgin Media was listed by Ofcom as signed up to the automatic compensation scheme.
Vodafone was listed by Ofcom as signed up to the automatic compensation scheme.
Zen Internet was listed by Ofcom as signed up to the automatic compensation scheme.
Participating companies provide compensation in the situations specified by the scheme.
Automatic-compensation amounts increase each year in line with inflation.
Delayed-repair compensation applies when service has stopped working and is not fully fixed after two full working days.
The listed delayed-repair amount is £10.34 for each calendar day the service is not repaired.
Missed-appointment compensation applies when an engineer does not attend a scheduled appointment or it is cancelled with less than 24 hours' notice.
The listed compensation is £32.31 per missed appointment.
Delayed-start compensation applies when a provider promises to start a new service on a particular date but fails to do so.
The listed delayed-start compensation is £6.46 for each calendar day of delay.
Unless an exclusion applies, compensation can remain payable when the problem is caused by an event beyond the customer or provider's control.
Extreme weather is listed as an example of an event beyond the customer or provider's control.
Strikes are listed as an example of an event beyond the customer or provider's control.
Third-party acts are listed as an example of an event beyond the customer or provider's control.
When landline and broadband both lose service at the same time, the scheme provides only one compensation payment.
The scheme covers all residential fixed broadband and landline products.
Unless otherwise agreed, compensation is provided as a credit on the customer's bill.
The compensation credit should be received no later than 30 calendar days after the relevant resolution, appointment or cancellation event.
For loss of service, the 30-day period runs after the service is resolved or terminated.
For a missed appointment, the 30-day period runs after the appointment date.
For delayed service start, the 30-day period runs after the delay is resolved or the service is cancelled.
A provider may offer an alternative form of compensation of the same or higher value if it explains the bill-credit value.
For a delayed start or missed engineer appointment, participating providers pay automatically without customer action.
For a stopped service, the customer must report the fault to the provider.
An initial £10.34 is payable if the service remains unfixed two full working days after the fault report.
A further £10.34 is payable for each full day the service remains unfixed after the initial threshold.
Loss caused by equipment or activity within the home is listed as an exclusion.
Breaking the terms of the contract is listed as an exclusion.
Compensation may be excluded when the customer caused the failure or prevented resolution.
When claiming an exception, the provider is expected to explain its reasons clearly and continue acting in the customer's best interests.
Where automatic compensation is legitimately not paid, a customer without service should not be charged for the service not received.
After 30 days of an automatic-compensation event, a provider can notify the customer that payments will stop after a further 30 days.
After a cease notification, the provider must take reasonable steps to offer a suitable alternative service.
If a suitable alternative service cannot be provided, automatic-compensation entitlement continues.
A customer who believes compensation was wrongly withheld should raise it with the provider, and unresolved complaints can go to an Ofcom-approved ADR service.
The Ofcom provider-rules summary was published on 19 July 2023.
The Ofcom provider-rules summary was last updated on 25 April 2025.
The page summarises major telecoms regulations, guidance and voluntary schemes for phone and broadband providers.
The page does not include every requirement that may apply to a provider.
Providers of electronic communications networks and services must comply with applicable General Conditions to provide services in the UK.
The scope section at the start of each General Condition identifies which providers and services it applies to.
General Conditions are structured around service type and customer type.
Each provider must determine which General Conditions apply to its services and customers.
The EECC-derived protections include provision of information in contracts.
The EECC-derived protections include transparency, comparison tools and publication of information.
The EECC-derived protections include quality of service.
The EECC-derived protections include contract duration and termination.
The EECC-derived protections include protections for end-users with disabilities.
The EECC-derived protections include switching and porting.
The EECC-derived protections include bundled offers.
New switching and porting rules came into effect on 3 April 2023.
Under One Touch Switch, residential landline and broadband customers need only contact their new provider to switch.
Providers serving individuals, qualifying small businesses and qualifying not-for-profit organisations must maintain compliant complaints procedures.
The complaints procedures must meet the minimum standards in the Ofcom-approved complaints code of practice.
Covered providers must belong to an alternative dispute resolution scheme.
Customers can use the provider's ADR scheme free of charge.
Ofcom identifies CISAS and Communications Ombudsman as the two ADR schemes.
General Condition C5 requires clear and effective policies and procedures for treating vulnerable customers fairly and appropriately.
Specific services for disabled customers include priority fault repair, text relay and free directory enquiries.
Power-cut guidance expects a solution enabling access to emergency organisations for at least one hour.
The Ofcom broadband-complaints news release was published on 23 July 2026.
Ofcom reported that complaints about major broadband providers had fallen to their lowest recorded level.
The latest complaint figures covered January to March 2026.
Ofcom stated that broadband complaints peaked at 40 per 100,000 customers in 2011.
Ofcom reported an all-time low of six broadband complaints per 100,000 customers in Q1 2026.
Ofcom says complaint data can help customers compare providers when considered alongside price, availability and quality.
Ofcom is unable to act on individual complaints through this aggregate complaints dataset.
TalkTalk was the most complained-about broadband provider in the Q1 2026 release.
Plusnet and Sky generated the fewest fixed-broadband complaints in the Q1 2026 release.
Collectively, complaints about major landline, broadband, mobile and pay-TV providers decreased in Q1 2026 compared with Q4 2025.
